We combine our diagnosis with examination of fire governance from fire-prone countries and transdisciplinary practitioner knowledge to propose ten principles for aligning fire policy with social-ecological realities. These principles offer a pathway beyond blanket suppression towards legitimate, adaptive and context-specific fire governance across sectors, institutions and scales.

title: Forest loss is increasingly driven by international consumption
abstract: Deforestation remains one of the greatest obstacles to limiting global warming, yet the economic mechanisms linking global supply chains to final consumers are poorly understood. Fine-scale satellite monitoring tracks where forests are lost, but rarely reveals who ultimately drives this loss through consumption. We further apply machine learning techniques to identify key socioeconomic drivers behind consumption-induced forest loss. Our results indicate that 38.15% of global forest loss—equating to approximately 5.01 Mha of the 13.12 Mha total in 2022—is embodied in international final demand, with five countries (Brazil, the United States, China, Indonesia, and Russia) accounting for 48.16% of global deforestation. China and Russia exhibit polarizing trends that amplify global forest pressures. Among the evaluated socioeconomic determinants, urbanization, manufacturing intensity, and domestic economic and conservation capacities emerge as the primary factors characterizing cross-national patterns of forest loss. This integrated framework offers a robust, data-driven foundation for advancing global forest conservation and promoting equitable responsibility across international supply chains.

title: Economic incentives for conifers may limit broadleaf expansion in climate-adaptive European forests
abstract: Forests are increasingly affected by climate change, highlighting the necessity of adaptive management to sustain ecosystem services. Yet adaptation is complicated by the interplay between ecological and socioeconomic considerations. We used an informed questionnaire to survey a selected group of forest professionals across different European sites, focusing on how perceptions of climate and socioeconomic change drive adaptive management choices. Here we show that professionals broadly agree on the negative impacts of climate change, with drought emerging as the dominant high-risk factor, while perceived socioeconomic change reflects rising timber demand and prices alongside higher operational costs. Professionals rank species diversity, mixing broadleaf and conifer species, and assisted natural regeneration as the priority adaptive measures, yet anticipated timber price increases lead a quarter of respondents to favor maintaining or increasing conifer shares. Economic expectations can change adaptation choices, highlighting a tension between ecological resilience and socioeconomic priorities that forest policy needs to address.

title: A revised early Jurassic to Albian chronology for dinosaur evolution in tropical Asia
abstract: The Mesozoic deposits of the Khorat Plateau in Thailand have yielded a rich but chronologically unclear record of dinosaur evolution. Here, we use detrital zircon U-Pb dating to establish precise ages for these deposits. The Nam Phong Formation, once thought to include some of the oldest sauropodomorphs, is now dated to the Pliensbachian stage of the Early Jurassic (ca. 190 Ma), at least 20 million years younger than previously assumed. The fauna of the Phu Kradung Formation, known for eusauropods and allosauroids, spans the Kimmeridgian to early Berriasian stages (ca. 155-140 Ma), covering the Late Jurassic to earliest Cretaceous. The diverse Sao Khua Formation dates to the Hauterivian–Barremian stages (ca. 130-120 Ma), while a shift to ornithischian-dominated communities occurs in the Aptian–Albian Khok Kruat Formation (ca. 120-100 Ma). This revised timeline shows that basal sauropodomorphs are significantly younger than assumed. It repositions Thai dinosaur assemblages within the global evolutionary framework, aligning their changes with faunal changes observed elsewhere and filling a critical gap in tropical fossil records.

title: Niche differentiation and functional complementarity between rare and abundant taxa sustain grassland soil bacterial diversity
abstract: Soil bacterial communities are central to grassland ecosystem functioning, yet how abundant and rare bacteria taxa differ in ecological strategies, community formation, and environmental responses remains unclear. Here we show, using 278 soil samples from grasslands across China, that these groups have contrasting but complementary ecological roles. Abundant taxa are mainly adapted to nutrient-poor conditions, tolerate a wider range of environments, and are shaped largely by random ecological processes. Rare taxa are more often associated with nutrient-rich conditions, occupy narrower environmental niches, and are governed more strongly by environmental selection. Machine-learning analyses identify pH and aridity index as the main drivers of diversity and community assembly in both groups. Predicted functions also differ: abundant taxa contribute more to carbon fixation, whereas rare taxa play greater roles in nitrogen cycling. Abundant bacterial functions depend mainly on geography and community composition, whereas rare bacterial functions rely more on diversity and respond more strongly to environmental change, highlighting their complementary contributions.

title: Rapid urban land uplift enhanced by crustal faults during groundwater recovery
abstract: Urban land subsidence driven by groundwater extraction is widespread, but the processes governing how groundwater recovery translates into spatially variable surface uplift remain poorly understood. We use satellite geodesy and multi-decadal groundwater observations to measure vertical land motion in Greater Osaka, Japan, where aquifers are intersected by a dense network of crustal faults. We observe widespread surface uplift at rates up to 12 mm/year, organized into distinct domains separated by sharp boundaries. Uplift rates vary abruptly across domain boundaries, which coincide with mapped faults. Where no faults are mapped, abrupt spatial changes in uplift rate suggest the presence of previously unrecognized buried faults. Uplift rates are positively correlated with groundwater-level rise in wells screened at depths up to 600 m, while deformation modelling indicates dominant uplift sources are shallower than 500 m. Our analysis suggests crustal faults act as hydraulic barriers to lateral groundwater flow, localising vertical land motion during aquifer recovery, with implications for groundwater management, infrastructure stability, and land-use planning in urban basins worldwide.

title: North Atlantic chlorophyll blooms modulate European hydroclimate and terrestrial productivity
abstract: Marine and terrestrial ecosystems are usually treated as separate components of the global carbon cycle, and whether variability in ocean biology reaches plant growth on land has remained unclear. Here we show that phytoplankton blooms in the high-latitude North Atlantic are linked to summer productivity across central Europe. During bloom years, pigments absorb more of the incoming sunlight within the shallow late-summer mixed layer, warming the sea surface. This warming accompanies higher pressure near the bloom and lower pressure over Europe, strengthening the westerly winds that carry moisture inland. Central Europe becomes wetter, and gross primary productivity rises by roughly 15–20% during the growing season. Experiments with a chlorophyll-interactive Earth system model support an active role for chlorophyll: when chlorophyll is held at its climatology, sea-surface temperature anomalies still develop, but the European productivity response is largely absent. Variability in marine ecosystems is therefore a potentially important pathway shaping productivity on land.

title: Overlooked contribution of organic alkalinity in Arctic Ocean margins biases ocean acidification estimates
abstract: Organic alkalinity has been recognized as a potentially substantial fraction of total alkalinity in coastal waters. However, conventional assessments of ocean acidification typically neglect its contribution when calculating pH and aragonite saturation state, potentially biasing the derived values. Here, we present elevated organic alkalinity in Arctic margins, and show that failure to account for it introduces substantial biases in calculated [H + ] (1% – 51%) and aragonite saturation state (1% – 117%) in the Svalbard fjords, Tanafjorden, and the Barents Sea Opening, with potential implications for the broader Atlantic sector of the Arctic margins. Regional projections based on Earth system model outputs further indicate that accounting for organic alkalinity leads to a larger and faster pH decline. These results indicate non-negligible biases in conventional ocean acidification assessments for Arctic margins and highlight the need to account for organic alkalinity in coastal waters and beyond.

title: Lake eutrophication increases unprotected organic carbon pools in sediments
abstract: Reactive iron oxide-bound organic carbon (Fe–OC) is a key pathway for long-term carbon burial, but its effectiveness under increasingly widespread eutrophication remains uncertain. Here we show that Fe–OC accounts for 16% of total organic carbon and buries at ~14 Mt C yr −1 in lakes globally, equivalent to ~27% of the marine Fe–OC sink despite lakes covering only ~1.25% of marine area. However, bloom-prone lakes exhibit lower Fe–OC content and contribution to sedimentary organic carbon than non–bloom-prone lakes. Field observations and incubation experiments further reveal that bloom-induced redox fluctuations and low-aromaticity algal organic matter inputs jointly accelerate Fe–OC turnover and reduce organic carbon loading on Fe minerals, causing Fe–OC losses of up to ~68%. These findings suggest that eutrophication weakens the long-term carbon burial capacity of lakes by increasing unprotected organic carbon pools in sediments, necessitating reevaluation of their contributions to the global carbon budget.

title: Coupled Sb-Hg isotopes reveal mixed basement and deeply recycled mantle-related metal sources for the South China antimony belt
abstract: Understanding the sources of metals in hydrothermal ore systems is fundamental for improving exploration models. However, direct tracers of metal sources remain limited, especially for large, low-temperature deposits. Here we apply coupled antimony (Sb) and mercury (Hg) isotope analyses to Sb deposits from South China, the World’s largest antimony metallogenic province. The dataset reveals substantial variability in δ 123 Sb (−0.64 to +0.69‰), δ 202 Hg (−1.86 to +2.08‰), and Δ 199 Hg (−0.20 to +0.14‰). These data support a model involving two metal sources, namely a deep, recycled mantle-related reservoir and Precambrian basement metamorphic rocks. Our results demonstrate that coupled Sb and Hg isotopes provide a potentially powerful tool with which to identify the metal sources for Sb ore deposits, and that their application may help refine models for these deposits globally and help decode the dynamic interplay between Earth’s interior and crustal metal cycling.

title: Future methane measurement campaigns require basin-specific sampling strategies
abstract: Methane emissions from the oil and gas sector follow right-skewed, heavy-tailed distributions, making it hard to accurately quantify average emissions with a limited number of measurements. In this study, we probe the statistical implications of sampling (i.e., measuring) from these right-skewed, heavy-tailed distributions using six US oil and gas basins as an example. For each basin, we provide a minimum sample size that bounds error in the average emission rate estimate introduced by sampling variability. We find that the largest emissions drive sample behavior, and by extension, sample size requirements; samples will underestimate (overestimate) average emissions if super-emitters are observed below (above) their true frequency. Importantly, we show that very large sample sizes can be necessary to mitigate this sampling effect. Furthermore, we find that a one-size-fits-all sampling strategy across basins is suboptimal; differences in super-emitter characteristics between basins necessitate a more tailored sampling approach.

title: Long-term, national-scale records of landslide persistence and dynamic hazard in a mountain landscape
abstract: As mountain populations grow and exposure to hazard increases, understanding the dynamic hazard posed by landslides is essential. However, our ability to constrain landslide hazard is limited by relatively few good-quality datasets that are often collected across small geographical areas. These datasets typically focus on specific triggering events, such as earthquakes or rainstorms, further complicating assessments of landslide hazard through time. To better capture landslide hazard through space and time, long-term datasets over large extents are needed. Here, we analyse a 22-year record of landslide occurrence to decipher the dynamic nature of the hazard posed by landslides in Nepal. We find that recurrent or persistent landslides dominate national-scale patterns of landsliding, accounting for c. 80% of all visible landslides at any given point in time. Of new landslide areas, only half occurred in locations >30 m away from other landslides. These findings emphasise the importance of also considering pre-existing landslides when assessing hazard. Individual triggering events, including both earthquakes and rainfall, leave a distinctive footprint visible at the national scale in metrics such as landslide density, persistence, and recurrence. Such metrics add significant value to multi-temporal landslide inventories and provide a basis for mitigation efforts, particularly where resources are limited.

title: Seasonal predictability of spring solar resources and wind-solar variability across the United States
abstract: The rapid expansion of solar and wind energy across the United States is increasing the demand for reliable seasonal forecasts to guide energy planning and grid operations. Here we show high seasonal prediction skill for springtime solar energy resources over the southwestern United States using a state-of-the-art seasonal forecast system. We identify two leading sources of solar predictability: a dominant component linked to primary El Niño-Southern Oscillation conditions, and a secondary component associated with El Niño-Southern Oscillation diversity and tropical Atlantic variability. Together, these components explain the spatial structure of forecast skill and its underlying physical drivers. State-level evaluations show robust solar prediction skill in high-resource states. The forecast system also captures the compound behavior of wind-solar variability and historical co-fluctuations associated with seasonal energy droughts and surpluses. These results provide a physically interpretable foundation for integrating seasonal forecasts into wind-solar energy planning and compound risk management.

title: Aridity-driven shifts in plant–microbial diversity relationships across the arid and semi-arid grasslands of northern China
abstract: Climate change-driven aridification threatens above- and belowground biodiversity, yet how the relationships between plant diversity and soil microbial diversity change along aridity gradients remains unclear. Here, we conducted a 4,000-km field survey across arid and semi-arid grasslands in northern China. We show that soil conditions, plant diversity, and microbial diversity exhibit sequential threshold responses along the aridity gradient. Beyond these thresholds, plant, bacterial, and fungal diversity generally decline, whereas archaeal species diversity increases. As aridity increases, the negative effects of soil salinity on plant, bacterial, and fungal diversity become stronger, whereas soil salinity shows increasingly positive associations with archaeal species diversity. Plant–bacteria and plant–fungi diversity relationships strengthen in drier regions, whereas plant–archaea relationships become decoupled. These findings show that aridity acts as a strong environmental filter, selecting stress-tolerant species and restructuring plant–microbial diversity coupling in a taxon-specific manner, and highlight the importance of aridity-dependent biodiversity coupling for shaping ecosystem resilience in arid and semi-arid grasslands under ongoing aridification.

title: Strong latitudinal contrasts in global wet/dry patterns since the Last Glacial Maximum and under future warming
abstract: Understanding regional wetting and drying under global warming remains challenging. Here we show, using global climate simulations and 191 records of past climate, that terrestrial moisture changes over the past 21,000 years follow a pronounced latitudinal pattern. Our reconstruction shows progressive wetting at high northern latitudes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the pre-industrial period. By contrast, many regions dominated by mid-latitude westerly winds are wetter during cold periods, whereas low-latitude monsoon regions are generally wetter during warm periods. These contrasts arise from seasonal changes in precipitation and evaporation and shifts in atmospheric circulation caused by changing ice sheets, greenhouse gas concentrations, and incoming solar radiation. A similar latitude-dependent structure appears in modern observations. Future simulations project drying across many subtropical and mid-latitude regions, but wetting at high latitudes and in monsoon regions. Continued warming is therefore likely to strengthen global differences between drying and wetting regions and expand water stress in vulnerable drylands.

title: Circularity measures enhance resilience of net zero pathways for agriculture
abstract: Reducing environmental impact of agriculture is paramount for sustainable food production. Development of a circular bioeconomy can contribute to environmental objectives, yet the interaction of circularity measures with net zero strategies is poorly understood. Using integrated modelling and 12 key performance indicators, we assess the sustainability and resilience of two simulated circular strategies implemented within a business as usual and three net zero greenhouse gas emission pathways for Ireland’s land sector. Two circularity strategies were designed: Energy-focused circularity maximised domestic feedstock utilisation for bioenergy production via anaerobic digestion. Feed-focused circularity minimised imported (overseas) inputs to national livestock systems. Net zero requires large-scale transformation across the land sector. Circularity moderately enhances greenhouse gas emission reductions through energy and livestock feed substitution but considerably strengthens the resilience of net zero pathways by lowering dependence on imported fertilisers, feeds and/or energy (depending on the circularity strategy). This work highlights opportunities to embed circularity within net zero land use strategies to improve resilience.

title: Insect outbreak progression over three years shapes biogenic volatile emissions in a mountain birch forest
abstract: Geometrid moth outbreaks are important natural disturbances in mountain birch ( Betula pubescens ssp. czerepanovii ) forests of northern Fennoscandia and are expected to intensify with climate change. Impacts of these outbreaks and moth herbivory on biogenic volatile organic compound (VOC) emissions of birch remain unquantified despite the importance of VOCs in plant-herbivore interactions and atmospheric chemistry. Here, we quantify in situ VOC emission responses of mountain birch ( n = 256) to naturally increasing geometrid herbivory across three consecutive growing seasons. We show that VOC emissions increased with rising herbivore pressure across the years, culminating in the outbreak, during which early-season VOC emissions were higher than at peak herbivory. At peak herbivory, birch emitted more complex VOC blends, indicating seasonal shifts in composition. Following the outbreak, a second leaf flush sustained emissions of some VOCs. Our findings demonstrate that VOC emission rates and compositions are dynamically linked to leaf phenology and herbivory intensity across multiple years.

title: Cascading fishery collapse associated with thermal habitat degradation, marine heatwaves, and predator influx
abstract: Global climate change and intensifying marine heatwaves contribute to abrupt fishery collapses. We investigate the fishery collapse of the Japanese flying squid ( Todarodes pacificus ) in the East Sea (Sea of Japan), which provides an early warning for climate-driven species replacements in warming oceans. Using multi-decadal observations (1993–2025), we identify a teleconnection where an intensified early-summer La Niña amplifies autumn–winter marine heatwaves within major fishing grounds. Sequential mediation analysis reveals that rising ocean temperatures drive the squid collapse through three interconnected pathways: gradual habitat degradation from long-term warming, acute thermal stress from marine heatwaves, and an ecological trade-off linked to the rapid influx of a warm-adapted predator ( Seriola quinqueradiata ). Climate model projections indicate unabated warming will increase the risk of the regional squid fishery reaching a zero-catch state by the 2040 s across multiple emissions scenarios. These findings underscore the urgent need for transboundary, climate-adaptive management.

title: Herbaceous leaf hydraulic trade-offs shape ecosystem function across the Mongolian Plateau
abstract: Plant hydraulic traits are fundamental to ecosystem drought responses, yet their integrated roles in mediating community-level functions remain unclear, especially for widespread herbaceous plants in drylands. Through a systematic investigation of herbaceous communities at 306 sites along a precipitation gradient of 152–411 mm across the Mongolian Plateau. We reveal that a community-wide trade-off between plant hydraulic efficiency and safety fundamentally organizes ecosystem function. Increasing aridity drives a strategic shift from efficiency- to safety-oriented traits. This governs a core functional trade-off: hydraulic efficiency enhances aboveground biomass by supporting greater photosynthetic carbon assimilation but reduces water-use efficiency and ecosystem stability, whereas safety traits exhibit the opposite pattern. Our quantified trait-based framework explains substantial variance in biomass (43%), water-use efficiency (40%), and ecosystem stability (60%). These findings establish a predictive mechanism for vegetation dynamics and provide essential insights for resilience-focused ecosystem management.

title: Climate warming amplifies coastal hypoxia response to extreme river discharge
abstract: Extreme hydrological events are critical drivers of coastal hypoxia, yet their impacts remain poorly constrained under future warming. Coastal oxygen depletion occurs when physical oxygen supply fails to offset biological oxygen demand, with stratification, nutrient enrichment, and warming further intensifying oxygen loss. Here, we quantify coastal oxygen responses to extreme discharge events using a three-dimensional hydrodynamic–biogeochemical model driven by high-resolution regional climate simulations for the Ariake Sea, Japan. Under a climate scenario 4 K warmer, extreme discharge magnitudes increase by 6.9% and 10.0% for 50- and 100-year return periods, respectively, relative to the historical baseline. This leads to a 33.2% increase in mean hypoxia duration (95% confidence interval: 11.7–55.3%, p < 0.01) for events within the 50–100-year return period range, while the additional increase in hypoxia duration from +2 K to +4 K warming is limited. Climate-driven intensification of extreme discharge strengthens stratification and prolongs hypoxia, with intensified conditions near estuaries and persistent low oxygen offshore, demonstrating that warming amplifies hypoxia and underscoring the need to integrate extreme events into coastal climate adaptation.

title: Baseflow dominates river flow during droughts across the global streamflow network
abstract: Hydrological droughts occur when rainfall shortages reduce water storage in catchments, leading to delayed and prolonged low-flow conditions. How strongly baseflow supports river flow during droughts and whether this buffering remains stable under climate warming remain uncertain across regions. Using global streamflow gauge observations, terrestrial water storage information, and CMIP6 simulations, we quantified the drought-sustained fraction (DSF), representing the fraction of drought-period streamflow contributed by baseflow, and the additive baseflow buffering index (BBI), which measures the departure from the climatological baseflow index (BFI). Under severe meteorological drought, 74.2% of stations showed a positive BBI, indicating stronger relative baseflow dominance, whereas 12.7% showed little change and 13.1% showed a decline in the baseflow fraction. BBI increased with low-flow severity and streamflow deficit, while baseflow retention declined, indicating that quickflow generally decreased more rapidly than baseflow. Present-day flow partitioning also constrained future slow-flow behavior, underscoring the importance of storage-release processes in sustaining river flow during drought.

title: Fluid inclusions establish natron as a key astrobiological target on Enceladus
abstract: Saturn’s moon Enceladus is a priority target for both NASA Flagship and ESA Large-class (L4) missions, as it possesses the three essential ingredients for life: liquid water, a source of energy, and all essential (CHNOPS) elements. As Enceladus’s ice crust is geologically active, future missions must understand its habitability through the lens of cryogeochemistry; yet the phase behaviour of Enceladus-type solutions is poorly constrained. Here, we investigate the freezing behaviour of an Enceladus-type Na-Cl-CO 3 solution using combined synchrotron X-ray computed microtomography and diffraction. We report the observation of fluid inclusions in cryogenic natron (Na 2 CO 3 .10H 2 O), a mineral predicted to occur both on and within Enceladus. We show that natron precipitation traps and preserves pockets of parent fluid, providing a window into the geochemistry of Enceladus’s interior and establishing natron as a mineral of high astrobiological importance. Consequently, we argue that future missions must have the capability to identify natron at the surface and that direct sampling should prioritise fresh plume deposits where natron is abundant due to its potential to trap and preserve signatures of life.

title: Marine arsenate evolution during Proterozoic oxygenation events and implications for biological phosphate metabolism
abstract: Earth’s atmosphere and oceans experienced two major episodes of ocean-atmosphere oxygenation that transformed the planet and shaped the evolution of the oxygen-rich biosphere between 2.45 and 0.541 billion years ago (Ga). These changes increased the abundance of oxidized chemicals in seawater, but their distribution and effects on the availability and utilization of essential nutrients remain poorly understood. Here we show that these oxygenation events were accompanied by stepwise increases in marine arsenate content—a toxic compound that closely resembles phosphate and interferes with its biological use. Arsenate concentrations rose during the first global oxygenation event and again after the end of the Sturtian global glaciation. Our results suggest that seawater contained much higher arsenate relative to phosphate than today for much of early Earth’s history, likely restricting biological access to phosphate. After the Sturtian glaciation, increasing phosphate availability lowered the arsenate-to-phosphate ratio, reducing arsenate toxicity and enabling more efficient phosphate use in shallow coastal seas, thereby supporting the expansion of oxygen-dependent life.

title: Carbon source and pollutant matching shapes microbial succession and removal regimes under electrochemical redox control
abstract: Electro-assisted bioreactors provide redox-controlled platforms for removing recalcitrant industrial organics, yet empirical co-substrate dosing often causes carbon–pollutant mismatch, diverting electrons and carbon fluxes into non-productive sinks. Here, we systematically pair three carbon sources with three representative pollutants to determine how carbon identity shapes microbial succession, interaction networks, and removal performance under coupled resource–stress gradients. Across nine pairings, successional trajectories and network configurations diverge reproducibly, yielding up to ~4-fold differences in pollutant removal. Co-substrates reshape niches and interspecies dependencies, redirecting metabolic routing and resulting in three succession regimes: pollutant-dominated, co-dominated, and carbon-dominated. Removal is most strongly associated with niche occupancy and ecological interactions ( r = −0.853, p < 0.01), supporting network-level emergence. Overall, this study provides an ecology-informed basis for tailoring carbon dosing to pollutant context, shifting from degrader-focused dosing to a network-centric strategy that supports decision-oriented control for smart, low-carbon wastewater management in electro-assisted and related anaerobic systems.

title: Fire-derived ozone intensifies carbon loss in Amazon forests under extreme droughts
abstract: The Amazon rainforest is a vital contributor to the removal of anthropogenic carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Ozone (O 3 ) is an atmospheric pollutant that reduces carbon dioxide uptake by vegetation. Yet the degree to which variability in ozone, elevated by anthropogenic-derived fire activity, and climate contribute to changes in Amazon forest productivity remains poorly understood. Here, we employ a land surface model to quantify the interannual variability of fire-derived ozone damage across the Amazon and explore its coupling with extreme drought and stomatal responses. We estimate that fire-derived ozone damage increases carbon losses by approximately one quarter of direct fire emissions, revealing a potentially important indirect pathway by which may fires amplify carbon loss. Notably, our simulations suggest high fire activity during extreme droughts, such as in 2024, likely result in ozone damage despite extensive stomatal limitation, highlighting the urgency to reduce deforestation and forest fire as the climate changes.

title: Satellite altimetry reveals heterogeneity in global flood peak timing and its shifts
abstract: Flood peak timing (FloPT) is a key indicator of hydrological responses to climate change. Yet global FloPT assessments is limited by sparse and uneven in-situ discharge observations. Here, we demonstrated the capability of satellite altimetry to estimate FloPT worldwide and presented the global map of observed FloPT, with a dramatic improvement in spatial coverage, especially in Global South countries. Altimetry-based FloPT shows distinct behaviors in snowmelt-dominated and precipitation-driven regions. Moreover, FloPT trends during 2008-2025 vary globally and within individual basins. 52.2% of the virtual stations and 27 of the 50 largest river basin outlets exhibit earlier FloPT. Earlier flood peaks are pronounced at high latitudes and elevations, consistent with accelerated snowmelt. Delayed peaks occur in the upper Mississippi, southern Amazon, and central Congo, consistent with shifts in precipitation maxima. Human water management also shapes abrupt FloPT changes, with stronger regulation constraining shifts. These results demonstrate the value of dense satellite altimetry resolving FloPT variability, particularly in remote and data-scarce regions.

title: Chlorophyll extremes during a surface marine heatwave in a seasonally stratified shelf sea
abstract: Marine heatwaves are increasing in frequency and intensity globally against a background of long-term climate warming, yet their impacts on subsurface biogeochemistry in temperate shelf seas remain poorly constrained. Here, we present high-resolution in situ observations of chlorophyll during a Category IV marine heatwave in June 2023, collected using an autonomous ocean glider in a seasonally stratified shelf sea. Surface chlorophyll exhibited a rapid but short-lived enhancement, increasing from <1 mg m⁻³ to >5 mg m⁻³ and briefly exceeding the climatological ±2σ range by up to 40%. In contrast, subsurface chlorophyll showed a sustained enhancement, with concentrations within the subsurface chlorophyll maximum increasing from typical post-bloom values of 1–2 mg m⁻³ to >3 mg m⁻³ and episodic peaks exceeding 9 mg m⁻³. This intensification was accompanied by an increase in depth-integrated chlorophyll, reaching 140 mg m⁻². Accelerated bottom mixed-layer warming and strengthened horizontal temperature gradients are consistent with a possible influence of horizontal transport processes, while elevated surface irradiance may also have contributed. These findings highlight the importance of sustained, vertically resolved observations for detecting ecosystem responses to climate extremes.

title: Catchment hydrologic function is widely time-variant
abstract: Catchment hydrologic function describes how meteorological conditions are transformed into streamflow. Whether this transformation is stable or varies from event to event, and what controls that variability, remains unknown at the global scale, limiting confidence in flood-risk and water-security assessments. Here, we analyze about 1.7 million runoff-producing events across 4838 catchments on six continents. We classify each event by its water-input type (rain, snowmelt, or rain-on-snow) and by its antecedent soil moisture (dry, moderate, or wet). These two descriptors together define the event’s hydro-meteorological conditions. We summarize each catchment’s dominant hydro-meteorological event type in the dormant and growing seasons separately, and find a wide diversity of dominant types across the global catchment population. We then quantify, for each catchment, the extent of event-to-event time-variance in the precipitation–streamflow transfer function that represents catchment hydrologic function. Time-variant catchment hydrologic function is pervasive: 95.6% of catchments in the dormant season and 99.0% in the growing season show moderate to strong event-to-event variation, and even catchments experiencing highly similar hydro-meteorological conditions across events remain functionally time-variant. Within-catchment spatial heterogeneity in hydro-meteorological conditions modulates this variation. Greater time-variance in hydrologic function is associated with greater event-to-event variation in a catchment’s runoff response.

title: Grazing-related disturbance decouples aboveground and belowground responses in the Eurasian meadow steppe
abstract: Grazing is among the most pervasive disturbances in grasslands, yet it remains unclear whether the Intermediate Disturbance Hypothesis (IDH), which predicts peak biodiversity at intermediate disturbance, extends from plant to belowground multitrophic communities. Across a grazing-related disturbance gradient in the Eurasian meadow steppe, we show that plant communities followed the IDH, with unimodal responses in diversity, biomass, and stability, whereas soil multitrophic communities followed a different trajectory. Soil multitrophic α diversity was insensitive to disturbance, yet β diversity peaked under moderate disturbance, accompanied by reduced network complexity and a shift toward positive associations, indicating belowground community reorganization consistent with the stress-gradient hypothesis. These contrasting responses were associated with reduced plant-derived carbon subsidies, including lower dissolved organic carbon and a shift toward more recalcitrant dissolved organic matter. Our findings reveal that the IDH does not generalize across trophic compartments, calling for integration of belowground multitrophic dynamics into grassland resilience frameworks under global change.

title: Arctic climate tipping points under delayed CO2 emissions mitigation
abstract: The Arctic is warming more than three times faster than the global average – driven by increasing CO 2 emissions – yet its response to the cessation of these emissions remains uncertain. We analyze 6-member ensembles of an Earth system model in which CO 2 emissions are set instantaneously to zero at cumulative emission totals ranging from 800 to 2000 PgC. While global mean temperature stabilizes after CO 2 emissions cessation, we find that the Arctic exhibits nonlinear and bifurcating behavior: either continued warming and sea-ice loss (below 1700 PgC), or abrupt cooling and sea-ice expansion (above 1700 PgC). The cooling results from a near-collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation, causing reduced poleward ocean heat transport and amplifying lapse-rate and surface-albedo feedbacks. This collapse occurs when CO 2 emission mitigation is delayed and global-mean temperature exceeds the 2 ∘ C Paris Agreement target. Our results suggest stochastic tipping behavior modulated by the increased greenhouse gas forcing, triggering an abrupt transition to an alternative Arctic climate state.

title: Assessing the potential and cost of enhanced rock weathering in China
abstract: Large-scale carbon dioxide removal is essential for carbon neutrality, but current options face constraints. Enhanced rock weathering is a promising alternative, yet its viability at a national scale in China remains unquantified. Here we show, using a spatially explicit analysis across China’s croplands, that a single-year basalt application could remove 0.44–0.79 billion tonnes of CO 2 by 2100, at a net life-cycle-adjusted cost of 127–226 US dollars per tonne of CO 2 removed. Particles finer than those typically used commercially provide the most favorable balance between removal potential and cost. Multi-year application has the potential to contribute 5–30% of China’s negative emissions needs by 2060, with priority areas in Northeast, Central-South, and East China. As an initial spatially resolved assessment, this study supports considering enhanced rock weathering in China’s carbon-management portfolio and motivates field trials and coupled soil–river geochemical modeling to constrain weathering, downstream carbon retention, and losses.

title: Onset of zircon decomposition during saprolitic weathering
abstract: Zircon is conventionally considered as refractory in supergene environments, enabling the preservation of geochemical records for tracing various Earth’s processes and the use of the zircon structure as a nuclear waste form. However, how refractory zircon is during weathering, especially when crystalline and in an early stage of weathering, is unknown. In this study, we demonstrate that crystalline zircon would start to weather during an early-stage saprolitic weathering. Nano-scale examination reveals that weathering of zircon proceeds through dissolution of primary, crystalline zircon and precipitation of secondary, amorphous zircon. Non-formula elements, like U, Th and heavy rare earth elements, are uptake and structurally incorporated in this process. Thereby, metamictisation of the zircon would accelerate and eventually promote the dissolution of zircon. In supergene environments, zircon would steadily weather, calling for further evaluation on the geological and environmental applications of zircon.

title: Land-atmosphere feedback amplifies circulation-dominant fire weather risk over eastern Siberia
abstract: Wildfires in eastern Siberia have intensified significantly in recent decades. This intensification is closely linked to rising vapor pressure deficit (VPD), a key indicator of fire weather risk. Previous studies have shown that atmospheric circulation increases VPD through subsidence-induced warming and drying, but the extent to which the circulation-driven VPD increase is realized through land–atmosphere feedback remains unclear. Here we show that atmospheric circulation explains about 60% of the 2004–2024 summer VPD trend over eastern Siberia, while circulation-triggered land-atmosphere feedback provides a major amplification pathway, accounting for about 42% of the circulation contribution. Mechanistically, reduced Laptev sea ice concentration favors a regional anomalous anticyclonic circulation over eastern Siberia, suppressing precipitation and depleting soil moisture. The resulting soil drying shifts surface energy from latent toward sensible heat, further amplifying regional VPD. These findings reveal a key land-surface pathway through which circulation intensifies fire weather risk and provide a broader framework for understanding similar changes in other fire-prone regions.

title: Distinct drivers control trace metal distributions through the Atlantic Ocean
abstract: Trace metals (TMs) including iron, manganese, cobalt, nickel, copper, zinc, cadmium, and lead have important biogeochemical roles in the ocean. However, the controlling factors of TM distributions have not yet been quantified and investigated on an ocean scale. Here we take a holistic approach to demonstrate that transport through water masses formed in high latitudes can explain 60–90% of dissolved TM distributions and >75% of TM inventories in the interior Atlantic. Water mass signatures were slightly modified by sinking organic matter remineralization mainly for iron, cobalt, nickel, cadmium, scavenging removal for iron, manganese, cobalt, lead, and hydrothermal inputs for iron and manganese. Our approach allowed prediction of the baseline TM distributions through the Atlantic at high spatial resolution. Through quantification, our findings emphasize the important role of large-scale oceanic circulation in determining global TM distributions once the water mass endmembers are set, despite the distinctive geochemical behaviors of the assessed TMs. Climate-related changes in a future ocean that impact endmember concentrations or relative water mass contributions may therefore perturb downstream TM inventories and ultimately affect ocean productivity and ocean carbon pump.

title: Episodic isolation of the Arctic Mediterranean from the North Atlantic during late Pleistocene glacials
abstract: It has been proposed that the Arctic Ocean and Nordic Seas (“the Arctic Mediterranean”) were not only episodically covered by an ice shelf during late Pleistocene glaciations, but disconnected from the North Atlantic and filled with freshwater. Originally based on the widespread occurrence of marine sediments with intervals barren of 230 Th xs (a function of salinity) and low in cosmogenic 10 Be (interpreted as ice cover), this interpretation is highly debated. Alternative explanations state that sediment pulses could instead have diluted both isotopes. Here, we trace the connection between the Arctic Mediterranean and the North Atlantic using reactive 10 Be/ 9 Be, a water mass tracer resilient to sedimentation variations. We find uniformly low 10 Be/ 9 Be that coincide with the 230 Th xs -minima and more than one order of magnitude below the coeval North Atlantic, consistent with an isolated Arctic Mediterranean. Our findings suggest a highly dynamic coupling between the Arctic Mediterranean and the North Atlantic, opening questions about its impact on global climate.

title: Impact of climate change on the photovoltaic power potential in Sweden across 21st century
abstract: Solar photovoltaic generation strongly relies on weather conditions, which will be affected by future climate change. Traditional methods for estimating photovoltaic generation potential often overlook detailed installation factors and snow impacts, leading to inaccuracies in high-latitude areas. We assess future photovoltaic system performance in Sweden using a validated photovoltaic installation model that incorporates air temperature, radiation and snow conditions. Applying this model to four Swedish cities under low- and high-emission climate change scenarios and three climate simulations, we project an approximate 5% increase in photovoltaic generation relative to the historical period with optimal installation angle. The combined effects of air temperature and snowfall are as crucial as solar radiation for photovoltaic generation in Sweden, so the photovoltaic generation change will be relatively limited by 2100. Optimized tilt angles are obtained for all the four cities, which could increase photovoltaic generation by 3-6% compared to the commercial angle. The findings also provide valuable insights into photovoltaic potential in a changing climate.

title: Social vulnerability amplifies global inequality in urban heat risk
abstract: Assessing urban heat risk is essential for developing heat adaptation and mitigation strategies. A key challenge in global-scale risk assessments is the common assumption of spatially homogeneous social vulnerability, often due to data constraints. Yet, the extent to which this assumption underestimates global climate inequality remains unclear. Here, we conduct a comparative heat risk assessment across 1,029 global cities during 2000–2019 by introducing a multidimensional social vulnerability index. Results reveal increasing urban heat risk worldwide, with the upward trend in the Global South nearly five-fold that in the Global North. We demonstrate that the traditional homogeneous assumption leads to a nearly 65% underestimation of North-South inequality in long-term heat risk. Furthermore, intraregional inequality measured by the Gini index is larger within the Global North and is underestimated by nearly 15% under the homogeneous assumption. Our study quantifies systematic bias in existing global heat risk assessments, providing a foundation for advancing climate justice in a rapidly warming world.

title: Baltic Sea sediment bacterial communities show asymmetric and incomplete recovery after reciprocal temperature change translocation
abstract: Marine coastal systems are important for global biogeochemical cycling and are particularly sensitive to climate change effects due to their shallow depths, which results in rapid heat transfer to the sediments. Here we used one-year reciprocal in situ translocations of sediments between a Baltic Sea long-term (>50 years) warming-influenced bay and a nearby unaffected control bay to predict how the sediments and their associated bacterial communities may respond to future climate change and whether those changes were reversible. Geochemical parameters, methane plus sulfate profiles, and 16S rRNA gene-based bacterial diversity and community composition show partial convergence of the sediment-parameters to the translocated environment, suggesting climate change will rapidly alter bacteria communities of Baltic Sea coastal sediments. However, more pronounced responses in the control to the heated bay translocation direction suggest that while a return toward present-day conditions may be possible if climate change is reversed, such a recovery may be incomplete or require a longer time than one year.

title: Physics-informed deep learning links geodetic data and fault friction
abstract: Fault slip modeling, based on laboratory-derived friction laws, has significantly enhanced our understanding of fault mechanics. Agreement between model predictions and observations supports the hypothesis that observed slip diversity, including fast earthquakes and slow transient slips (Slow Slip Events; SSEs), originates from frictional heterogeneity. However, quantitative assessments of frictional heterogeneity from geodetic observations while fully incorporating fault mechanics are lacking due to the difficulties of high-dimensional optimization. In this study, we aim to address this gap using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to link frictional heterogeneity with geodetic observations. PINNs employ a neural network to represent the spatially variable frictional properties, making their estimation feasible. Targeting the 2010 Bungo SSE in southwest Japan, our estimation reveals heterogeneous friction coinciding with localized SSE nucleation in southwest Shikoku, and subsequent westward propagation. The calculated fault slip of SSE successfully reproduces the spatio-temporal pattern of observed surface displacements. This PINN-based inversion provides a mechanically consistent fault slip model validated through quantitative comparison with observations. Furthermore, we forecast the future fault slip evolution, demonstrating the importance of assimilating observations spanning multiple SSE cycles. Our results demonstrate the potential of PINN for advancing understanding of fault mechanics and enabling physics-based fault slip forecasting.

title: Weathering-derived calcium supports carbon storage in grassland soils
abstract: Dark colored grassland soils, known as Mollisols, are intensively farmed and rich in organic matter, and hence have an important role in the carbon cycle. Organic carbon storage in Mollisols may result from interactions between organic matter and calcium released by carbonate and silicate weathering. Here we test this hypothesis by using a geochemical model to simulate calcium release from weathering in soils across the USA. We find that calcium released by mineral weathering is associated with soil organic carbon storage and that this effect is stronger in Mollisols than in non-Mollisols. Our model also shows that agriculture has increased calcium inputs to cultivated USA Mollisols 4-5 fold, indicating that humans have fundamentally changed the geochemical conditions that sustain organic carbon in these soils. By implication, moderating the quantity of and timing of calcium release may help to preserve and restore carbon in the world’s most intensively farmed landscapes.

title: Ocean thermal inertia sustains a tropical Pacific mean state shift under net zero
abstract: The tropical Pacific plays a pivotal role in global climate, and changes in its mean state and in the El Niño Southern Oscillation can substantially alter regional hydroclimates with major economic and societal impacts. Yet, its response to different emission pathways remains poorly constrained. Here we assess changes in the tropical Pacific mean state and variability under high emission and net zero scenarios, using climate model simulations spanning centennial to millennial timescales. Under transient warming, the tropical Pacific shifts towards an El Niño-like mean state. Following emission cessation, continued warming of the Southern Ocean and deep ocean sustains this mean state for centuries, driving persistent El Niño-like rainfall anomalies and more frequent extreme El Niño events even as atmospheric carbon dioxide declines. Changes in ENSO amplitude, by contrast, are non-monotonic and more model dependent. Key aspects of tropical Pacific change are therefore effectively irreversible on multi-centennial timescales, and net zero emissions slow further change without restoring pre-industrial conditions.

title: U.S. oil and gas methane emission intensity declined 2019–2024 with little indication of federal policy impact
abstract: The U.S. federal government undertook a historic legislative effort to regulate methane emissions from the oil and gas sectors beginning in 2021 through the Inflation Reduction Act and Waste Emissions Charge. Despite a substantial rollback of these regulations in subsequent years, U.S. oil and gas methane emissions during this policy window are largely uncharacterized. Here we estimate changes in U.S. methane emissions both before and directly after this policy window (years 2019 to 2024) using an inverse model constrained by satellite observations. Overall, we find that oil and gas methane emissions decreased by 0.58 [0.30, 0.96] Tg from 2019 to 2023, but increased by 0.21 [-0.06, 0.53] Tg in the years following the new federal policy (2023–2024). We find that methane emissions intensity declined by 11.1% [9.3%, 13.6%] from 2019 to 2024, likely as a result of gradual technological and operational developments, and existing federal regulations.

title: Impact-based flood-damage assessment in Japan under longitudinal typhoon-track perturbations and levee-height variations during Hagibis (2019)
abstract: Impact-based flood-damage assessment integrates hydrometeorological information with vulnerability and exposure data to generate comprehensive evaluation of flood damage. This study uses the Integrated Land Simulator to assemble an impact-based flood-damage assessment framework for Typhoon Hagibis (2019), one of the most powerful typhoons to strike Japan in recent years. To systematically evaluate how typhoon-track position and levee height influence flood damage, we conduct longitudinal typhoon-track perturbation experiments and levee-height variation scenario analyses. Here we show that the flood damage is highly sensitive to small typhoon-track shifts, with a 0.2° longitudinal shift causing an average damage difference of 83.3 billion JPY. A 1.0° eastward shift causes the highest damage in Kanto and across Japan, mainly around Tokyo, while 1.6° and 0.4° westward shifts produce the greatest damage in Kinki and Chubu, mainly around Osaka and Nagoya, respectively. The levee-height sensitivity experiments show an average flood-damage reduction of approximately 9.1 billion JPY for each 10% increase in levee height.

title: Geochemical clustering reveals cryptic eruptions and tephra correlations from Antarctic fumarolic ice-cave archives
abstract: Volcanic deposits preserved within Antarctic fumarolic ice caves provide rare access to sub-ice eruptive records hidden beneath the ice cap. Here we present the first integrated textural, petrological, and geochemical characterisation of 21 tephra samples from three summit ice caves at Mount Melbourne (Northern Victoria Land, Antarctica). Major and trace-element glass compositions, combined with published datasets, were analysed using multivariate statistical workflows. Dimensionality reduction and clustering identified a distinct compositional group with no known equivalent in the existing Mount Melbourne record, suggesting that at least one previously unrecognised Holocene eruption occurred within the investigated Fumarolic Ice Caves. Correspondence between Fumarolic Ice Cave deposits and volcanic signatures in marine sediment, englacial sequences, and other proximal-distal records refined Mount Melbourne’s eruptive history and strengthened tephra correlations across archives. More broadly, sub-ice tephra archives can reveal hidden eruptive histories relevant to volcanic hazard assessment in polar regions.

title: Seasonal wetting and drying dynamics drive greenhouse gas emissions across Australia’s river network
abstract: Streams and rivers are major contributors to global emissions of carbon dioxide and methane, yet seasonal hydrological variability in discharge and river surface area is often not fully represented in large-scale emission estimates. Here, we integrate riverine and dry riverbed carbon dioxide and methane data with geospatial data of the Australian drainage network to predict emissions at a monthly time-step. We show that flowing Australian rivers emit a total of 48.5 teragrams of carbon dioxide and 0.28 teragrams of methane annually, with dry riverbeds adding 13.9 teragrams of carbon dioxide, according to integrated river emission measurements and geospatial drainage network analysis. Spatiotemporal emission patterns closely follow variations in river surface area, with contrasting seasonal pulses from tropical regions in the wet season and temperate regions in winter. These results highlight the importance of hydrological dynamics, particularly the seasonal expansion and contraction of river networks, in governing riverine emissions across Australia.

title: Global ice loss drives source-independent amplification of sea-level rise at Pacific and Indian Ocean Small Island Developing States
abstract: We quantify the spatial pattern (“fingerprint”) of sea-level rise caused by mass loss from the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets and from glaciers worldwide through 2100. Using ensembles of ice-sheet and glacier mass-balance projections and gravitational, rotational, and deformational sea-level modeling, we calculate normalized sea-level fingerprints and their impacts on Small Island Developing States. We show that Small Island Developing States in the Pacific and Indian Oceans are located within persistent sea-level-rise hotspots where the ice-melt contribution to local sea-level rise systematically exceeds the global mean by up to ~ 24%. This amplification emerges regardless of whether meltwater originates from Greenland, Antarctica, or the global glacier system. We identify a source-independent and geographically systematic amplification of sea-level rise affecting some of the world’s most climate-vulnerable nations .

title: Remote sensing of aquatic nutrients from proxy estimation to integration with process models
abstract: Leveraging its capability for large-scale, repeated monitoring, remote sensing has increasingly supported nitrogen and phosphorus estimation in surface waters. However, the evolution of this field from proxy-based nutrient retrieval to integration with process-based models remains insufficiently synthesized. Here we review remote sensing approaches for estimating aquatic nutrients, with emphasis on their roles in supporting process-based modeling, and compare their methodologies, applications, and limitations. At the watershed scale, remote sensing supports land use mapping and pollution load estimation, identifying nutrient sources and constraining transport simulations. At the lake scale, it provides continuous observations and water quality products that inform hydrodynamic and water quality models. At the field and interface scales, remote sensing helps identify hotspots of nutrient loss by capturing the heterogeneity of management practices. Despite these advances, nutrient estimation remains constrained by proxy relationships and spatial scale. Future research should integrate remote sensing with hydrodynamic and biogeochemical models to constrain nutrient fluxes and improve mechanistic understanding of aquatic nutrient cycling.

title: Nickel isotopes in Apollo and Chang’e soils reveal widespread micrometeorite-driven processing of the lunar regolith
abstract: Micrometeorite bombardment is a fundamental surface process on the Moon and other airless bodies, driving elemental evaporation, isotopic fractionation, and material mixing in surface regoliths. Here, we report high-precision stable Ni isotope data for lunar soils returned by the Apollo (11, 12, 14, 15, 16, and 17) and Chang’e (5 and 6) missions, covering geographically and geologically diverse lunar terrains. The analyzed soils show δ 60/58 Ni values of 0.345‰ to 1.280‰ (relative to NIST SRM 986), generally heavier than lunar basalts and the inferred bulk silicate Moon, indicating widespread heavy Ni isotope enrichment during surface processing. Together with published Chang’e-5 drill-core data, these results demonstrate that micrometeorite-driven Ni isotope fractionation is widespread across the lunar surface. Local variability, however, reflects additional controls. The relatively low δ 60/58 Ni values of the immature Apollo 12 soils are consistent with limited cumulative micrometeorite processing, whereas the mature Apollo 16 soils have high Ni concentrations and Ni/Co ratios, indicating additional compositional overprinting by Ni-rich material. Stable Ni isotopes, particularly when combined with regolith maturity and Ni/Co ratios, therefore provide a sensitive tracer of micrometeorite-driven lunar surface processing and its local overprinting.

title: Abrupt permafrost thaw overwhelms vegetation-driven erosion reduction in sediment export on the Tibetan Plateau
abstract: Vegetation greening and abrupt permafrost thaw are reshaping sediment dynamics across the Tibetan Plateau, yet their relative effects on sediment delivery remain poorly quantified. Here we show that retrogressive thaw slumps are disproportionately important sediment sources, with erosion rates two to three orders of magnitude above undisturbed landscapes and source-to-channel connectivity generally exceeding 60%. Combining multi-decadal satellite observations, high-resolution topographic differencing and cold-region hydrological modelling, we quantify the competing effects of thaw-slump sediment supply and greening-induced erosion reduction. During 2000–2022, thaw slumps delivered more than four times as much non-ice sediment to channels as was reduced by greening, compensating for declining glacier-derived sediment and contributing to increased downstream suspended sediment export. Across permafrost regions, approximately 1.2‰ thaw-slump coverage represents an upper-bound threshold above which thaw-slump sediment delivery exceeds greening-induced sediment reduction. These results show that spatially limited abrupt thaw can outweigh widespread vegetation recovery in regulating sediment delivery from warming permafrost landscapes.

title: Regulatory frameworks need to distinguish persistent from transient plastic fragments
abstract: Plastic particles below a diameter of 5 mm are often grouped together under the label ‘microplastics’ in current Environmental Impact Assessment protocols, regardless of their environmental half-life. We argue for a fundamental shift in nomenclature and regulatory frameworks: microplastics should be regulated according to degradability, with separate categories for transient and persistent particles. Plastic particles below a diameter of 5 mm are often grouped together under the label ‘microplastics’ in current Environmental Impact Assessment protocols, regardless of their environmental half-life. This Comment argues that microplastics should be regulated according to degradability, with separate categories for transient and persistent particles.

title: Subglacial landforms as proxy for offshore freshened groundwater in formerly glaciated margins
abstract: Offshore freshened groundwater (OFG) is a significant yet underexplored component of the global water cycle, and its spatial distribution, particularly its links to past glacial processes, remains poorly constrained. The southeastern North Sea, characterized by extensive tunnel valley networks, provides an ideal setting to test how Pleistocene meltwater shaped offshore groundwater systems. Using newly acquired time-domain controlled-source electromagnetic data integrated with high-resolution seismic reflection surveys, we present a resistivity-based mapping of OFG in this region. The models reveal a laterally continuous OFG body with resistivities of 8–14 Ω·m, extending across multiple stratigraphic units and well beyond individual subglacial landforms. This configuration is best explained by subglacial meltwater flushing of sediment porewaters during Pleistocene glaciations. Subsequent preservation was aided by density contrasts that limit vertical mixing and by fine-grained glaciomarine deposits sealing the system from above. The connection between resistivity anomalies and mapped subglacial landforms shows that the latter can serve as predictive proxies for OFG occurrence. These findings shift the perspective from OFG as isolated anomalies to regionally extensive systems linked to glacial processes, establishing subglacial landforms as a testable screening proxy for locating OFG in formerly glaciated margins worldwide.

title: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation sustains carbon sinks under warming Tibetan permafrost region
abstract: Symbiotic nitrogen fixation (SNF) by legumes is a major natural source of reactive nitrogen that supports ecosystem functioning and carbon sequestration. Warming across the Tibetan Plateau alpine permafrost region may trigger substantial shifts in vegetation composition and distribution, yet the consequences for ecosystem nitrogen inputs remain poorly understood. Here, using 1047 plant samples from 323 plots across the Tibetan Plateau and 15 N natural-abundance techniques, we quantify legume and non-legume nitrogen sources and regional aboveground SNF rates. Aboveground SNF is tightly linked to legume aboveground biomass, ranges from 0 to 7.43 g N m −2 yr −1 , and peaks at elevations of 3600–4000 m. At the regional scale, its spatial distribution largely coincides with recent decadal gains in aboveground biomass and plant nitrogen density. Process-based simulations show that removing SNF causes severe nitrogen limitation and shifts these ecosystems from a carbon sink to a source. Our findings highlight the important role of legumes in sustaining carbon sinks in Tibetan Plateau permafrost ecosystems.

title: Functional diversity complements taxonomical diversity in productivity-biodiversity relationships in freshwaters
abstract: Productivity is widely considered a key driver of biodiversity, yet whether taxonomic and functional diversity respond similarly to productivity gradients remains unclear. Using phosphorus as an indicator for productivity gradient, we compiled 78 freshwater datasets spanning > 30,000 sites globally to test how productivity–biodiversity relationships (PBRs) vary across diversity dimensions, trophic groups, and ecosystems. We show that PBRs are predominantly unimodal across taxonomic and functional dimensions, with slightly weaker curvature for functional diversity. Unimodal PBRs are more pronounced in producers than in consumers and show stronger curvature in lakes than in rivers. Functional reorganization also varies along the phosphorus gradient, with the clearest contraction in resource-related trait space and marked shifts in community functional centroids. Climatic, geographic and human land-use gradients further modify PBR shape. These findings indicate that predicting biodiversity responses to productivity benefits from considering functional diversity, ecological context, and broad-scale environmental gradients.

title: Author Correction: Sustainable palm oil certification inadvertently affects production efficiency in Malaysia
abstract: Correction to: Communications Earth & Environment https://doi.org/10.1038/s43247-025-02150-2 , published online 12 March 2025

title: Effusive sedimentary volcanism experimentally reproduced under Martian-like conditions
abstract: Rapid boiling, cooling, and freezing are commonly assumed to rapidly quench metastable liquid eruptions exposed to near-vacuum planetary environments, influencing both sedimentary volcanism on Mars and cryovolcanism on icy worlds. However, how these coupled phase transitions govern eruptive processes remains largely unknown. Here we show experimentally that boiling instead sustains coupled ballistic-effusive mud eruptions under Martian-like pressure conditions (~4.5 mbar). Using an ice-sealed metastable reservoir, we reproduced subsurface-driven eruptions initiated by internally generated boiling-induced overpressure. Eruptions evolved systematically from short-lived ballistic fountains toward episodic effusive emplacement accompanied by coherent mud-flow formation. Ballistic transport redistributed liquid mud around the vent and promoted proximal accumulation that subsequently coalesced into sustained flows despite ongoing cooling and freezing. Numerical modeling further demonstrates that erupted mud would remain largely unfrozen during ballistic transport under Martian gravity conditions. Together, our results show that rapid boiling does not suppress sedimentary volcanism under low-pressure conditions, but instead actively sustains eruptive transport and surface emplacement. These findings provide new constraints on this process on Mars and establish a broader physical framework for metastable liquid eruptions across the Solar System.

title: Warming since the Last Glacial Maximum amplifies Northern Hemisphere drought expansion driven by the Pacific Decadal Oscillation
abstract: The Pacific Decadal Oscillation (PDO) modulates decadal precipitation patterns, and subtropical troughs act as rainfall “commanders”. However, whether PDO influences precipitation variability by affecting these troughs remains unclear. By combining reanalysis data with present-day and Last Glacial Maximum (LGM) simulations, we reveal that PDO regime shifts regulate spring precipitation by altering subtropical trough positions and associated wind patterns. A negative PDO phase deepens the India-Burma trough and shifts its base ~1330 km equatorward, inducing northeasterly anomalies to its east that weaken moisture transport and suppress precipitation over East Asia. Concurrently, it shallows the North American subtropical trough and shifts its base ~560 km poleward, promoting a ridge development that reduces precipitation in water-stressed western North America. Notably, the 4-6 °C warming since the LGM has amplified the negative PDO drying effect, increasing affected area by 160% in East Asia and 57% in North America. These results clarify how the PDO regulates subtropical trough dynamics to shape spring precipitation, providing a mechanistic basis for drought risk assessments under similar warming magnitude to that projected for this century.

title: Free tropospheric halogen oxidation drives mercury deposition in the Asia Pacific region
abstract: Asian outflow represents 50% of global anthropogenic mercury emissions, but the atmospheric oxidation pathways controlling its deposition to the adjacent Pacific Ocean remain poorly constrained. Using multi-year snow and atmospheric mercury isotope measurements from Mt. Halla, Jeju Island, Korea, we delineate the mercury sources and oxidation pathways governing deposition to marginal Asia and the western Pacific. Mass-independent fractionation of even-number mercury isotopes (even-MIF; Δ 200 Hg) correlates with both air mass transport distance and trajectory altitude, indicating the importance of free tropospheric mercury photo-oxidation triggering even-MIF. Coupled anomalies between Δ 200 Hg and oxygen isotopes of nitrate (Δ 17 O(NO 3 - )) in snow indicate that reactive bromine, generated from debromination of local sea salt aerosol, sustains oxidative capacity in the free troposphere and drives active mercury deposition to Mt. Halla snow. Isotope mixing models quantify that halogen-mediated free tropospheric mercury oxidation (68%) exceeds near-surface oxidation (32%). Our results provide field-based evidence for a bromine-driven free tropospheric photo-oxidation mechanism regulating mercury deposition to Asia-Pacific ecosystems.

title: Regionalized greenhouse gas emissions and infrastructure requirements for future global iron and steel production
abstract: The steel industry accounts for approximately 7–9% of global greenhouse gas emissions, making it a key sector for decarbonization. Here, we quantify current and prospective greenhouse gas emissions from crude steel production facilities worldwide. Based on life cycle assessment, current greenhouse gas emissions of global crude steel production are around 3.7 gigatonnes carbon dioxide equivalent per year, highly concentrated in Asia. Depending on the future 2 ◦ C scenario in 2040, greenhouse gas emissions may decline by up to 70%, to 1.1–2.3 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per year. Also, we show that decarbonizing steel may require up to 90 million tonnes of hydrogen per year, 1.0 gigatonne of carbon dioxide storage per year, and/or electricity supply with up to 6,000 terawatt-hours per year, more than twice the European Union’s current electricity supply. Our results highlight the importance of regional context and the substantial infrastructure needs of low-carbon steel production.

title: Canadian lakes show contrasting phosphorus trends across climatic regions
abstract: Phosphorus regulates lake productivity and water quality, yet long-term changes in lake phosphorus and their climatic drivers remain poorly understood at continental scales. Here we show how total phosphorus changes across 15,240 Canadian lakes > 5 km 2 from 1984 to 2025 using a deep neural network trained with 35,452 field measurements and applied to 386,727 Landsat images. Arctic tundra watersheds show increasing phosphorus concentrations of 0.15 μg/L yr −1 , whereas boreal forest, temperate forest, agricultural and urban watersheds show declines of 0.07, 0.11, 0.16 and 0.12 μg/L yr −1 , respectively. Path analyses link northern increases to ground warming and soil erosion, consistent with permafrost-related phosphorus mobilization. Southern declines are associated with vegetation greening, hydrological change, and reduced human phosphorus inputs, while surface runoff remains important in agricultural and urban systems. These findings reveal contrasting climate-sensitive phosphorus trajectories and show that climate change can reinforce or counteract nutrient management gains, highlighting the need to integrate region-specific climate adaptation into lake management.

title: Low-carbon technologies support energy security by buffering energy price shocks
abstract: Energy supply crises matter because their economic impacts extend beyond energy markets. We argue that energy security should be understood by how energy systems transmit price shocks to the wider economy. Low-carbon technologies matter because, unlike fossil fuels, they dampen this transmission through the economy. Energy supply crises matter because their economic impacts extend beyond energy markets. This Comment argues that energy security should be understood by how energy systems transmit price shocks to the wider economy. Low-carbon technologies matter because, unlike fossil fuels, they dampen this transmission through the economy.

title: Persistent seasonal deoxygenation alters benthic metabolic processes and accelerates hypoxia feedbacks in the Baltic Sea
abstract: Nutrient enrichment and warming cause widespread costal deoxygenation, leading to hypoxia or even anoxia in bottom waters. The benthic-water-column-feedbacks that develop under persistent seasonal oxygen depletion and amplify hypoxia remain poorly constrained. A 15-month study of a seasonally hypoxic to anoxic costal system in the southwestern Baltic Sea combined water-column monitoring, sediment chemistry, metabolic rates and microbial analyses with historic data to reveal pronounced seasonal shifts in sediment processes. During winter oxygenation, organic matter degradation, fermentation, aerobic respiration, nitrate- and iron-reduction and microbial competition increased. Re-ventilation following anoxia did not reset sediment biogeochemistry, but initiated intensified oxygen consumption, microbial biosynthetic activity and anaerobic carbon re-cycling. Reactive ironoxyhydroxides became exhausted, the sulfidic zone shoaled and sulfate reduction and pyrite formation rates increased through fall. These processes reinforced benthic feedbacks, progressively reducing the sediment’s capacity to retain sulfide over years. This weakening of sedimentary resilience exacerbates sulfide accumulation in eutrophic costal environments with growing chances of sulfidic deep-water upwelling.

title: Microbially mediated interactions between enhanced weathering and carbon inputs shift soil organic carbon dynamics
abstract: Enhanced weathering, adding crushed silicate minerals to soils, is being explored as a way to draw down atmospheric carbon dioxide, but its effects on soil organic carbon remain uncertain. We show that olivine amendments change soil carbon cycling depending on time and on labile carbon availability. In a 55-week soil microcosm experiment, adding olivine alone reduces total soil organic carbon. Adding olivine with glucose initially suppresses microbial carbon uptake, but by week 55 instead boosts microbial biomass and mineral-associated organic matter more than glucose alone, while lowering respiratory carbon loss. These late-stage gains grow stronger alongside geochemical signs of mineral weathering. Nanoscale imaging shows that newly formed soil organic carbon accumulates within pre-existing organic and mineral microsites rather than directly on olivine or newly formed clay surfaces. Our findings suggest that when labile carbon is available, enhanced weathering can increase soil carbon storage primarily through microbial processing, rather than by creating new mineral surfaces for carbon to bind to.

title: Coupled responses of aboveground and belowground net primary productivity stability to nitrogen deposition in grasslands
abstract: The temporal stability of plant net primary productivity (NPP), defined as the ratio of temporal mean productivity to its standard deviation, is crucial for sustaining ecosystem services. Yet, little is known about whether the effects of nitrogen deposition on aboveground NPP (ANPP) stability are coupled with corresponding changes in belowground systems. Here we conducted a global meta-analysis based on 542 multi-year observations from 111 studies to assess the impacts of nitrogen deposition on the stability of ANPP and belowground NPP (BNPP). Nitrogen addition significantly decreased the stability of both ANPP and BNPP in a synchronized manner, reflecting a coupled response resulting from the allocation trade-off between mean ANPP and BNPP and their synchronized increase in variability. Further analysis showed that the declines in both ANPP and BNPP stability were associated with decreased plant species richness under nitrogen addition. Moreover, the negative responses intensified with longer treatment durations and higher nitrogen addition intensity. These findings highlight the importance of considering above- and below-ground interactions in future ecosystem management strategies under global change scenarios.

title: Drying and rewetting of riverbed sediments results in cold to neutral biogeochemical moments
abstract: Sediment respiration in streams/rivers impacts global biogeochemical cycles, yet is mostly studied under perennially-inundated conditions despite all river corridors having variably inundated areas and most streams going dry each year. Previous experiments observed sediment rewetting to cause elevated or suppressed aerobic respiration, indicating variation across studies. To deepen understanding, we conducted 21-day wet/dry experiments with sediments from 64 streams spread across the contiguous United States. Here we show that drying and rewetting sediments from perennial and non-perennial streams had near-neutral effects or suppressed O 2 consumption rates. These biogeochemical cold moments contrast previous studies that observed hot moments. Sediment texture and microbial activity explained variation in responses to rewetting, but this did not reveal why some studies observed cold moments while others observed hot moments. To solve this we propose a unifying conceptual model whereby hot and cold moments exist simultaneously upon rewetting by considering both dry-state and perennially-inundated reference points.

title: Bay of Bengal cyclones fuel non-monsoon extreme precipitation on the central Tibetan Plateau
